paragraphs: When maps connect several objects or domains, optimizing each map separately can leave their predictions inconsistent. Cycle consistency provides a shared constraint: following a sequence of maps around a loop should return to the starting point. Joint optimization uses these relationships to coordinate maps, including shape correspondences and neural networks connecting image domains.

The difficulty is deciding which loops to enforce. A graph can contain exponentially many cycles, making the choice of a manageable subset important for both efficiency and effectiveness. The paper introduces an algorithm that selects cycles and assigns them weights, with the objective of minimizing a condition number of the resulting joint optimization problem.

This turns cycle selection into a question about the numerical properties of the optimization problem. The selected constraints are intended to support effective joint fitting, rather than merely increase the number of enforced loops. Benchmark experiments support the approach for dense correspondences between 3D shapes and neural networks that predict dense image flows.
neurips-2019-a-condition-number-for-join.tldr: The paper selects and weights consistency cycles by an optimization condition number, with demonstrated benefits for shape matching and image-flow prediction.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares probability distributions through the cost of moving mass between them, but finding the exact minimum can be computationally expensive. This paper studies an additive approximation: the computed transport cost may exceed the optimum by a specified amount, delta. That makes the relationship between accuracy and computation central to the method.

The authors adapt a classical graph algorithm by Gabow and Tarjan and give a new runtime analysis. With n denoting the problem size and C the largest cost, the bound is O(n²C/delta + nC²/delta²). Each iteration uses a Dijkstra-type search followed by a depth-first search, and the iteration count is controlled by the ratio C/delta.

The resulting procedure brings familiar graph-search operations to transport approximation. Empirical results suggest execution times competitive with a sequential Sinkhorn implementation. The authors also report that their method quickly obtains solutions for very small additive errors, where the compared Sinkhorn algorithm slows because of numerical instability. These findings support the algorithm as a practical option when tight additive accuracy matters.
neurips-2019-a-graph-theoretic-additive-.tldr: A graph-search algorithm approximates optimal transport with a proved additive-error runtime bound and promising performance at tight error tolerances.

paragraphs: Perception combines uncertain sensory evidence with expectations about how the world works. In a changing environment, later observations can also alter the interpretation of an earlier event, a phenomenon called postdiction. The paper asks how a neural system could perform this revision while continuing to process information in the present.

The proposed framework uses a distributed distributional code, or DDC, to represent uncertainty. It extends that representation to carry implicit probabilistic beliefs about both current and past states. This allows new sensory evidence to inform beliefs about earlier events within an ongoing inference process, without requiring information to physically travel backward in time.

The authors show that the inference model can be learned efficiently from samples generated by an internal model of the world. Applied to stimuli associated with psychophysics experiments, the framework produces postdictive effects through an online inference mechanism. Its contribution is a neurally plausible account of how maintaining uncertainty about the past can support perceptual revision as further evidence arrives.
neurips-2019-a-neurally-plausible-model-.tldr: A neural uncertainty representation supports online perception that revises beliefs about past events when new sensory evidence arrives.

paragraphs: A software performance regression occurs when a code change makes a program perform worse. AutoPerf addresses the task of automatically testing for and diagnosing these regressions. The paper places this within machine programming: using learning methods to automate work involved in developing and maintaining software.

AutoPerf combines zero-positive learning, autoencoders, and hardware telemetry. Together, these provide a learning-based approach to interpreting measurements of program execution for regression diagnosis. The emphasis is on identifying performance bugs through observed execution behavior. Because collecting those observations itself consumes resources, profiling overhead is an important part of the reported evaluation.

The authors evaluate three types of performance regression across ten real performance bugs in seven benchmark and open-source programs. AutoPerf has an average profiling overhead of 4% and accurately diagnoses more bugs than the prior state-of-the-art approaches used for comparison. The authors also report no false negatives so far: within the reported experience, it did not miss a performance bug. That observation describes the evaluation record, rather than a guarantee for every future regression.
neurips-2019-a-zero-positive-learning-ap.tldr: AutoPerf combines learning and hardware telemetry to diagnose performance regressions, reporting 4% average profiling overhead and no false negatives so far.

paragraphs: Training a large neural network spends substantial computation calculating gradients for individual examples. AutoAssist starts from the observation that an example's contribution to improvement changes as training progresses. It therefore filters out examples estimated to offer relatively little marginal improvement, concentrating expensive gradient calculations on more informative examples.

The framework trains a lightweight Assistant alongside the main network, called the Boss. The Assistant estimates an example's importance for the Boss in its current state, and the batch generator uses that estimate to shrink the set of examples processed. Both models train asynchronously and without blocking each other, keeping the extra work from substantially offsetting the savings.

Experiments cover image classification with ResNets of different depths and machine translation with LSTM, ConvS2S, and Transformer models. The authors report significant reductions in training time and reductions of 30% to 40% in total operation count. The findings support adaptive example selection as a way to accelerate convergence by changing where training computation is spent as the model learns.
neurips-2019-autoassist-a-framework-to-a.tldr: AutoAssist uses a lightweight model to filter less useful training examples, reducing total operation counts by 30% to 40% in the reported applications.

paragraphs: BIVA addresses a performance gap between variational autoencoders and other generative models. Its central idea is to make effective use of a deep hierarchy of stochastic latent variables, allowing the model to represent complex relationships within data. Different parts of the hierarchy can capture different aspects of the distribution being learned.

The architecture combines a generative model with skip connections and an inference network whose stochastic path runs in both directions. This arrangement is designed to make the deep hierarchy useful for modeling complex covariance structure. The authors report state-of-the-art test likelihoods together with generated natural images that are sharp and coherent.

The paper also explores uses beyond image generation. It observes that BIVA can detect anomalies and attributes this ability to high-level semantic features extracted through the latent hierarchy. That explanation is the authors' interpretation of the observation. An extension to semi-supervised classification performs comparably to state-of-the-art generative adversarial network results, suggesting that the learned hierarchy can also support prediction when labels are only partly available.
neurips-2019-biva-a-very-deep-hierarchy-.tldr: BIVA combines a deep latent hierarchy with bidirectional inference to achieve strong generative performance and support anomaly detection and semi-supervised classification.

paragraphs: The paper connects two capabilities that are often developed separately: learning to recognize information in raw data and reasoning with symbolic knowledge. In abductive learning, a machine learning model converts observations into primitive logical facts. A reasoning component then uses domain knowledge to identify and correct facts that were perceived incorrectly.

Those corrections feed back into learning, so symbolic reasoning helps improve perception rather than simply consuming its outputs. The authors also propose a method for jointly optimizing the learning and reasoning models. This mutual interaction matters because errors in recognizing an input need not remain fixed before reasoning begins.

The demonstration uses images of simple handwritten equations. The system learns both to recognize numbers and to resolve unknown mathematical operations, bringing visual interpretation and reasoning into the same learning process. The authors report that the learned models generalize to longer equations and adapt to different tasks, beyond the capabilities of the state-of-the-art deep learning models considered. These results illustrate how domain knowledge can guide learning when recognizing symbols and understanding their relationships must happen together.
neurips-2019-bridging-machine-learning-a.tldr: Abductive learning jointly develops perception and logical reasoning, using symbolic knowledge to correct learned interpretations of handwritten equations.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization algorithms move through a sequence of parameter updates, but their behavior can also be studied through continuous-time models. This paper develops such formulations for first-order methods, including mini-batch gradient descent and variance-reduced algorithms. The purpose is to make their convergence and evolving dynamics easier to analyze mathematically.

The authors combine these formulations with stochastic calculus and Lyapunov analysis, which uses a quantity that tracks progress toward convergence. They derive convergence bounds for several types of nonconvex functions. They then show that the same Lyapunov arguments also apply in discrete time, yielding matching rates for the corresponding step-by-step algorithms.

The continuous-time viewpoint additionally provides an interpretation of learning-rate decay. Using Itô calculus, the authors prove that a decreasing learning rate acts as a change in the passage of optimization time, or equivalently as a stretching of the objective landscape. This connects a practical optimization choice to the dynamics of the model. The contribution therefore includes both convergence analysis and a mathematical account of how learning-rate schedules change SGD's evolution.
neurips-2019-continuous-time-models-for-.tldr: Continuous-time models yield convergence analyses for stochastic optimizers and explain decreasing learning rates as time warping or landscape stretching.

paragraphs: Adversarial perturbations alter inputs so that a neural network makes incorrect predictions. Transferability makes these attacks relevant even when an attacker cannot inspect a target model's internal parameters. This paper challenges the usual dependence on data from the target domain by demonstrating adversarial patterns that transfer across substantially different image domains.

The method trains a generative network with a relativistic supervisory signal to produce domain-invariant perturbations. The resulting perturbation function is instance-agnostic, rather than separately optimized for each target example. The authors show that a function learned from paintings, cartoons, or medical images can perturb ImageNet images successfully, reaching fooling rates as high as approximately 99% under the stated infinity-norm bound of 10.

The authors report state-of-the-art fooling rates in both white-box and black-box settings, as well as performance exceeding the instance-specific attacks considered. These findings provide evidence of shared adversarial vulnerabilities across the tested datasets and models. Their significance is that successful transfer need not depend on learning perturbations from the same domain as the eventual target classifier.
neurips-2019-cross-domain-transferabilit.tldr: A generative attack learns perturbations that transfer across image domains, demonstrating shared adversarial vulnerabilities in the tested networks.

paragraphs: An optimization problem can serve as a neural network layer when training can differentiate through its solution. This lets a model incorporate the structure expressed by that optimization problem. The paper addresses the difficulty of building such layers for new settings, where existing software had required relatively rigid formulations.

The authors introduce disciplined parametrized programming, a subset of disciplined convex programming. Every program in this subset can be decomposed into three components: an affine transformation from parameters to solver data, the solver itself, and another affine transformation back to the original problem's solution. They show how to differentiate efficiently through these components, providing analytical derivatives through the complete program.

The method is implemented in CVXPY 1.1, with differentiable layers for PyTorch and TensorFlow 2.0. Applications include linear machine learning models and stochastic control. The reported execution times are competitive with specialized differentiable solvers. The practical contribution is a more general route from a structured convex problem to a trainable layer, reducing the need to build a separate differentiation implementation for each application.
neurips-2019-differentiable-convex-optim.tldr: The paper makes a structured class of convex optimization problems usable as differentiable layers through an affine-solver-affine decomposition.

paragraphs: Representation learning often compresses an input while retaining enough information to reconstruct it. This creates a trade-off between the information preserved, called the rate, and reconstruction error, called distortion. The paper argues that familiar Gaussian assumptions make this trade-off tractable but can restrict the encoding, while generally providing only an upper bound on the actual compression rate.

Echo noise is a new, data-driven noise channel with a simple exact expression for mutual information for arbitrary input distributions. Mutual information measures how much information about the input survives in the representation. Having an exact expression lets the model regularize that quantity directly without relying on restrictive distributional assumptions of the kind highlighted in the paper.

The authors report improved log-likelihood bounds and rate-distortion performance that dominates beta-VAEs across the achievable trade-off range. They also show that Echo can outperform flow-based methods without training additional distributional transformations. These findings connect the encoding mechanism and exact rate control to improved representation learning, rather than treating the noise distribution merely as a mathematical convenience.
neurips-2019-exact-rate-distortion-in-au.tldr: Echo noise enables exact information-rate regularization in autoencoders and improves the reported trade-off between compression and reconstruction.

paragraphs: Off-policy prediction learns about one policy using experience collected under another. Importance sampling corrects this mismatch by reweighting updates, but those weights can make value-function updates highly variable. This paper explores moving the correction into the selection of experience, before the learning update is calculated.

Importance Resampling selects experience from a replay buffer and then applies standard on-policy updates. Importance ratios therefore do not appear in the update itself; the sampling distribution carries the correction. The authors analyze the method's bias and consistency, particularly in relation to Weighted Importance Sampling, making these statistical properties part of the comparison.

Across several microworlds, the method shows better sample efficiency and lower update variance than importance sampling and several approaches intended to reduce its variance. The comparisons include variants of Weighted Importance Sampling and V-trace. A further demonstration learns a value function from images in a racing simulator and improves over importance sampling. Together, these results support resampling as a useful alternative location for off-policy correction.
neurips-2019-importance-resampling-for-o.tldr: Importance Resampling corrects off-policy data through replay selection, producing lower-variance updates and improved sample efficiency in the reported tests.

paragraphs: Unitary recurrent neural networks constrain their recurrent transformations to address vanishing and exploding gradients in long sequences. That constraint raises a separate question: which input-output behaviors can such networks represent? The paper studies this representational issue by asking when a unitary network can exactly reproduce the behavior of another recurrent network.

For any contractive recurrent network using ReLU activations, the authors prove that a unitary recurrent network can implement the identical input-output mapping with at most twice as many hidden states. This is an exact equivalence result, not merely a statement that predictions can be made close. It establishes that the unitary constraint need not lose mappings from this contractive ReLU class when additional hidden states are allowed.

The activation function is decisive. For certain smooth activations, the authors show that some recurrent-network mappings cannot be matched by a unitary network, regardless of how many states it has. Experiments on slowly varying dynamical systems support the theoretical results. The findings therefore tie representational equivalence to the activation choice as well as the recurrent constraint.
neurips-2019-input-output-equivalence-of.tldr: Unitary RNNs can exactly match contractive ReLU RNNs with at most twice the hidden states, but equivalence fails for certain smooth activations.

paragraphs: Binarized neural networks use binary weights, yet their training commonly maintains additional real-valued quantities that accumulate small updates. These quantities are often called latent weights. The paper argues that understanding them as ordinary real-valued network weights obscures their main function in the optimization process.

The authors instead interpret latent weights as providing inertia during training. In this view, the accumulated information governs how resistant a binary weight is to change. The distinction matters because accumulating many small updates in a real-valued variable serves a different role when the network's usable weight has only binary choices. The paper uses this perspective to reinterpret existing training methods.

Building on that interpretation, the authors introduce Binary Optimizer, or Bop, designed specifically for binarized networks. They demonstrate its performance on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. The contribution combines a conceptual account of the training state with a concrete optimizer based on the needs of binary weights. It offers a basis for understanding and developing BNN training methods, rather than simply borrowing the interpretation of weights from real-valued networks.
neurips-2019-latent-weights-do-not-exist.tldr: The paper reinterprets latent real-valued weights as training inertia and introduces Bop, an optimizer designed for binarized neural networks.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning from a mixture of public and private examples, where differential privacy is required only for the private portion. Its question is how many examples of each kind are needed. Public data can assist learning without receiving the same protection, but the private examples must still be handled under the privacy requirement.

For a hypothesis class with VC dimension d, the authors show that agnostic learning to excess error alpha is possible using roughly d/alpha public examples and d/alpha² private labeled examples. Agnostic learning does not require the hypothesis class to contain a perfectly correct predictor. Crucially, the public examples can be unlabeled, so their usefulness does not depend on supplying additional public labels.

The public sample requirement improves from inverse-quadratic to inverse-linear dependence on the target error compared with the stated standard bound. The authors also establish a nearly matching lower bound through a reduction to private learning without public data. Together, the bounds describe both an achievable trade-off and a closely corresponding limit on the amount of public data needed.
neurips-2019-limits-of-private-learning-.tldr: The paper establishes nearly matching bounds on how public examples, even unlabeled ones, can assist differentially private learning.

paragraphs: The MaxGap problem asks where a collection of noisy quantities naturally divides into a higher group and a lower group. Each quantity is represented by an arm that can be sampled to estimate its mean. The desired split lies at the largest gap between adjacent means once those means are ordered.

Unlike selecting a predetermined number of top arms or applying a fixed threshold, the location of the division must be learned from the data. An arm's gap also depends on its neighbors, so sampling that arm alone is insufficient to resolve the comparison. The paper captures this dependence in a new hardness parameter governing sample complexity.

The authors propose elimination and upper-confidence-bound-style algorithms and prove minimax optimality. Their experiments find that the UCB-style methods use six to eight times fewer samples than nonadaptive sampling at the same error level. The result illustrates the value of directing observations toward uncertain neighboring relationships when the goal is to discover a natural separation, with applications including approximate ranking, noisy sorting, and outlier detection.
neurips-2019-maxgap-bandit-adaptive-algo.tldr: MaxGap algorithms adaptively find the largest separation between neighboring arm means, with minimax guarantees and substantial experimental sample savings.

paragraphs: A tensor organizes observations along several dimensions, and useful groups may exist along more than one of those dimensions. This paper studies how to recover that multiway block structure when the observed tensor is large and noisy. Such structure appears in settings including genomics, recommendation, topic modeling, and sensor network localization.

The authors introduce a tensor block model and a unified least-squares estimator. They establish statistical convergence and theoretical accuracy guarantees for the resulting clustering method, including partition consistency. This connects the fitted numerical model to the recovery of the underlying grouping, rather than assessing the model only by how closely it fits observed entries.

The method also includes sparse regularization to identify important blocks with elevated means, allowing the analysis to highlight particular groups of entries. It accommodates binary, continuous, and hybrid observations. Simulations and applications to two real datasets show better performance than the previous methods considered. The contribution combines a flexible model for several data types with theoretical support for recovering groups across multiple dimensions.
neurips-2019-multiway-clustering-via-ten.tldr: Tensor block models recover multiway clusters from noisy data, with statistical guarantees and a sparse extension for identifying elevated blocks.

paragraphs: Event sequences often mix several event types, with each occurrence potentially depending on earlier events of its own type or other types. Point processes model such sequences over time. This paper focuses on regressive point processes, which represent dependencies directly between an event and past events, rather than considering only isolated occurrence times.

The authors develop a nonparametric model based on Gaussian processes, with conditional Gaussian processes identified in the title. The aim is to represent dependencies that existing nonparametric Hawkes-process variants find difficult to capture. The central modeling question is therefore how flexibly the history of different event types can influence predictions about subsequent events.

The paper reports that the model better represents many commonly observed event sequences and demonstrates improved predictive performance against state-of-the-art baselines on multiple synthetic and real datasets. These findings support the proposed treatment of event dependencies in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a new model within the regressive point-process family, extending the available ways to describe how a mixed event history shapes future occurrences.
neurips-2019-nonparametric-regressive-po.tldr: A Gaussian-process-based regressive point process models complex event dependencies and improves prediction on the reported synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: ODE2VAE learns a compact representation of high-dimensional sequences together with a continuous-time model of how that representation changes. The two tasks are learned simultaneously: the model discovers an embedding for observed trajectories while inferring their latent dynamics. This connects representation learning directly to the problem of predicting movement through time.

Its defining structure separates the latent state into position and momentum components and evolves them through a second-order ordinary differential equation. That explicit decomposition gives the dynamics a particular organization, distinguishing it from recurrent sequence models and black-box ODE approaches. Deep Bayesian neural networks parameterize the probabilistic dynamics so the model can account for uncertainty.

The authors demonstrate the approach on motion capture, rotating images, and bouncing balls. They report state-of-the-art performance in long-term motion prediction and imputation, the task of filling in missing observations. These results support learning the representation and temporal evolution together, with an explicit second-order latent structure and probabilistic dynamics, for the sequence tasks evaluated.
neurips-2019-ode2vae-deep-generative-sec.tldr: ODE2VAE jointly learns sequence representations and uncertain second-order latent dynamics, reporting state-of-the-art long-term motion prediction and imputation.

paragraphs: Random-walk landing probabilities describe where a walk is likely to arrive after different numbers of steps. Generalized PageRank combines these probabilities with weights, making the weighting scheme important for extracting useful graph information. This paper studies how those weights should be chosen for expanding a seed into a detected community.

The authors provide a non-asymptotic analysis of landing probabilities and generalized PageRank on random graphs with independent edges. It describes convergence toward mean-field values without relying only on limiting behavior. For community detection under stochastic block models, they find that the predictive usefulness of landing probabilities declines substantially more slowly than earlier asymptotic findings had suggested.

That result motivates Inverse PageRank, which increases the weights assigned to the first few walk lengths. The weighting preserves more influence for steps that the analysis indicates still carry useful information. Experiments on synthetic graphs and large real networks show superior seeded community detection compared with the other generalized PageRank methods considered. The paper thus connects finite-size theoretical analysis to a concrete change in graph-based prediction.
neurips-2019-optimizing-generalized-page.tldr: Finite-size analysis motivates Inverse PageRank's increasing early-step weights, improving seeded community detection in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper develops a framework for making neural-network predictions with partially encrypted computation while protecting sensitive data. It combines functional encryption with adversarial training. Functional encryption lets a data owner authorize evaluation of a particular function on encrypted data, without requiring the owner to participate in the calculation itself.

The authors introduce an efficient functional-encryption scheme for quadratic functions and use it with neural networks that have quadratic activations at evaluation time. They analyze information leakage through the indistinguishability of data items sharing a label. This makes the privacy analysis sensitive to what a prediction reveals about individual inputs within the same class.

A further issue is the final thresholding operation used for classification, which several encryption schemes cannot handle. The proposed training method counters leakage of selected sensitive features by training against an adversary attempting to identify them. The authors report substantially improved privacy with almost no accuracy cost. The contribution combines restricted encrypted computation with learned protection against feature leakage, addressing privacy at both the computation and model-training levels.
neurips-2019-partially-encrypted-deep-le.tldr: Functional encryption and adversarial training enable partially encrypted neural predictions while reducing leakage of selected sensitive features.

paragraphs: In a recovering bandit problem, the expected reward from an option depends on how long it has been since that option was last selected. The relationship between waiting time and reward is unknown and must be learned. This changes the decision problem because choosing an option now also affects the circumstances under which it can be chosen later.

The learner therefore has to estimate more than one fixed reward value per option and plan beyond the immediate next choice. The paper explores Gaussian processes for learning these unknown reward functions and supporting planning. It also examines different definitions of regret, which provide different ways to quantify the performance of a policy in this evolving setting.

To reduce the computational demands of planning, the authors provide an optimistic approximation. Regret bounds and empirical studies complement the modeling and planning discussion. The contribution addresses the linked challenges of learning how rewards depend on time since use and scheduling future actions accordingly, rather than treating each arm as having a constant expected payoff.
neurips-2019-recovering-bandits-c8806418.tldr: Recovering bandits use Gaussian processes and optimistic planning to handle rewards that depend on the time since an option was last chosen.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning agent may have several ways to compress its observation history into a discrete state. Choosing a useful representation matters because the apparent dynamics depend on that choice. This paper studies online learning when such alternatives are available and at least one of them yields a Markov decision process.

The proposed algorithm, UCB-MS, learns while adapting to a Markov representation. Its performance is measured by cumulative regret relative to the optimal policy with the highest average reward in that representation. This benchmark asks how much reward the agent loses over time while resolving the representation and decision-making problem.

The authors prove an O(sqrt(T)) regret bound for communicating Markov decision processes, improving on the previously stated O(T^(2/3)) rate. The smaller growth rate means accumulated loss rises more slowly with the interaction horizon under the theorem's setting. The guarantee depends on the availability of a representation inducing an MDP and the communicating-MDP condition. Within that setting, the bound shows that the algorithm automatically adapts to the Markov model.
neurips-2019-regret-bounds-for-learning-.tldr: UCB-MS adapts among candidate state representations with O(sqrt(T)) regret when the stated Markov and communicating-process conditions hold.

paragraphs: The thresholding bandit problem asks which options have average rewards above a specified cutoff. Each trial provides information about one option, and the learner has a fixed total budget of trials. The objective is to allocate those observations so that the final classification places as many options as possible on the correct side of the threshold.

The paper introduces LSA, a simple anytime algorithm targeting aggregate regret, defined here as the expected number of misclassified arms. This objective counts errors across the collection of options. Describing the algorithm as anytime means it can provide a result when sampling stops, making it relevant when the available trial budget determines the stopping point.

The authors prove instance-wise asymptotic optimality: the optimality statement applies to each problem instance in the asymptotic regime. It does not assert exact optimality at every finite budget. They also report extensive experiments showing better performance than existing algorithms across varied scenarios. Together, the theoretical and empirical findings support LSA for efficiently classifying many uncertain reward means against a common threshold.
neurips-2019-thresholding-bandit-with-op.tldr: LSA classifies bandit arms against a reward threshold with instance-wise asymptotic optimality for the expected number of classification errors.

paragraphs: An image can support several valid captions that differ in both word choice and sentence structure. The paper argues that existing generative captioning approaches overlook these two sources of diversity. VSSI-cap explicitly models lexical and syntactic variation so that diversity is represented within the caption-generation process.

The model uses an encoder, a structured inference component, and a decoder. Its central component is a Variational Multi-modal Inferring tree, or VarMI-tree. Conditioned on visual and textual features, this tree infers latent variables for the two forms of variation through approximate posterior inference guided by a visual semantic prior. The decoder then combines visual information with these latent variables to produce captions.

Training jointly uses reconstruction loss and a divergence term that aligns the inferred posterior with the prior. This connects learning to reproduce captions with learning a structured distribution of possible expressions. Benchmark experiments show significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The contribution is to make word-level and sentence-level variation explicit parts of the latent model used for diverse image captioning.
neurips-2019-variational-structured-sema.tldr: VSSI-cap models word choice and sentence structure through a variational inference tree to generate diverse image captions.
